extracted.intended_audience: students, researchers, and practitioners interested in scientific method, induction, and experimental design (philosophy of science/empirical researchers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for carrying out inductive inquiry: how to observe, mentally decompose phenomena, vary circumstances, and design experiments so as to assign causes to effects reliably. Emphasizes the Composition of Causes, the limits of deductive prediction in chemistry/biology, and practical rules for observation and experimentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition of Causes
rubrics_metrics.description: When several agents (causes) operate jointly, the joint effect is identical with the sum of their separate effects provided the same law which expresses the effect of each cause acting by itself also correctly expresses the part due to that cause when they act together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle is exemplified in mechanical phenomena (principle of Composition of Forces). If satisfied, one can deduce conjunct effects a priori by 'casting up the results'. Example: two perpendicular forces produce displacement equal to the separate displacements each would have produced. Scoring note: applicable where causes do not alter one another's laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize heteropathic (non-compositional) cases
rubrics_metrics.description: In many combinations (notably chemical combinations and organized bodies) the joint action of causes produces effects heterogeneous to those seen when causes act separately; new laws may emerge which are not the sum of separate effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume deductive predictability from component properties in chemistry or life-science contexts. Example: hydrogen and oxygen produce water with properties unlike either gas. Anti-pattern: attempting to compute compound properties by mere summation of element properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine the mode of conjunct action before applying composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Before predicting joint effects, ascertain whether the joint action of causes will obey Composition (sum of separate effects) or will give rise to new laws (heteropathic).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This determination is fundamental: if the same law applies to causes separately and together, composition holds; if not, expect qualitatively new phenomena. Experimental designs should test which mode holds in the domain of interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know separate effects to predict joint effects
rubrics_metrics.description: To arrive a priori at correct predictions of conjunct agency, one must know what effect each cause would produce when acting separately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the individual effects are not known, deductive prediction of their combination is generally impossible. Thus design experiments to measure causes' isolated effects first.

rubrics_metrics.name: Varying the circumstances (Baconian rule / isolation)
rubrics_metrics.description: To discover which antecedents are connected with which consequents, follow the rule of varying the circumstances: obtain instances where antecedents occur apart from others or where consequents are found apart, so causal relations can be identified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the foundational rule of physical inquiry. Use either naturally occurring instances or artificially created ones (experiments). Ensure antecedents can be met apart from other conditions (isolation) to assign cause to effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental decomposition must precede physical separation
rubrics_metrics.description: The observer must mentally analyze complex antecedents and consequents into component parts to suggest the physical separations/experiments required to test causal relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carry mental subdivision as far as needed to see what observations or experiments are required, but no further than necessary. Be prepared to refine decomposition further as occasion requires. Anti-pattern: failing to mentally separate phenomena or making awkward/incorrect partitions that hinder experiment design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use experiment to produce controlled variations (experiment extends observation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Experiment is an immense extension of observation: it enables producing variations not found in nature and, in many cases, the precise variation required to discover a law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer experiments when natural instances do not supply needed variations (example: isolating oxygen to test respiration). Experiments allow the investigator to create instances suited to inductive inference and to observe causal relations under controlled changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observe phenomena in known/controlled circumstances ('take it home')
rubrics_metrics.description: When a phenomenon can be produced artificially, one can observe it in circumstances with which one is accurately acquainted—bringing the phenomenon 'home' for controlled study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This permits clearer attribution of antecedents and consequents because background conditions are known. Design experiments to control or record relevant background factors so observed effects can be reliably connected to manipulated causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware the axiom of proportionality of effects to causes
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposition that effects are proportional to their causes is only valid as a particular case of the Composition of Causes; it fails where augmentation of cause alters the kind of effect (thresholds, qualitative changes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume linear scaling without verification. Test for thresholds and qualitative transitions (e.g., heating: more heat may change expansion → melting → decomposition). Experimental design must probe for nonlinearity and regime changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat opposing causes as additive (including negatives)
rubrics_metrics.description: When concurrent causes tend to produce contrary effects, the joint result can still be the sum of their separate effects; the algebraic notion of addition (including negative quantities) applies to net effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze opposing influences by summing their separate effects (with appropriate signs). Example: inflow and outflow of a reservoir can be treated as additive (one positive, one negative) to find net change. Use this mental model to interpret canceled or net-zero observed outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek intermediate/derived laws for complex systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when compound systems exhibit emergent properties not deducible from elemental laws, there may exist simpler 'laws of life' or intermediate-level regularities derivable by induction that allow higher-level deductive reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In complex chemistry, physiology, or social phenomena, look for reproducible regularities at intermediate complexity (e.g., laws of definite proportions, isomorphism). Such discoveries can make these domains progressively more amenable to deduction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish raw observation from inference/imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: Good observers record what they actually see, not what they imagine or infer; they note kinds of circumstances and estimate degrees/quantities accurately rather than vaguely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid conflating observation with interpretation. Anti-patterns include: inattention (omitting facts), conflating observation with imagination, leaving quantities vague, and making improper partitions. Training and self-education improve observational skill, though there is no formal 'Art of Observing' in logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of an instance independent of how obtained
rubrics_metrics.description: The logical value of an instance for induction depends on the instance itself, not whether it was obtained naturally or artificially.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat naturally occurring and experimentally produced instances under the same inferential principles. Practical distinctions exist (experiments allow more and precise variations), but their inductive worth is determined by the instance's relevance to the causal question.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on material antecedents relevant to the phenomenon
rubrics_metrics.description: In designing observations/experiments, omit antecedents shown by experience to be immaterial to the result (e.g., planetary positions for a chemical experiment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct attention and resources to antecedents plausibly connected to the effect. Historical or metaphysical considerations (e.g., occult influences) should not be assumed relevant without empirical support; specificity increases experimental efficiency.
